claims.text: HfNbTaTiZr is a high-entropy alloy.
The target specimens contain approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The target specimens have minimal extrinsic defects and represent typical experimental samples.
The proposed model integrates ab initio phonon or energy-landscape data, oxygen-defect scattering rates, and local short-range-order effects.
The proposed model will accurately predict lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions separately.
The model will reduce relative thermal-conductivity prediction error by roughly 30% compared with traditional analytical models.
Experiments below 200 K show approximately comparable lattice and electronic heat-transport contributions in HfNbTaTiZr.
High-temperature measurements up to approximately 1200 K report total thermal conductivity of 10–17 W/(K·m).
Local chemical short-range order mediates phonon scattering.
Oxygen-induced defect sites mediate phonon scattering.
Local short-range order and oxygen-induced defects modify electron mobility.
Decoupling the two transport channels and learning scattering behavior from ab initio data and experimental calibration enables separate temperature-dependent phonon and electron predictions.
Accounting for site-to-site variations, defects, and departures from an ideal lattice improves transport prediction.
Existing analytical heat-transport models for the alloy rely on a single Debye temperature.
Existing DFT-based transport models assume ideal, defect-free crystals.
The proposed model is applicable to HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen controlled near 1 wt.%.
The model may not apply to substantially different compositions or processing conditions.
The claimed temperature applicability extends from below 200 K to approximately 1200 K.
Below 200 K, the model predicts approximately equal lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions.
At higher temperatures, the model predicts total thermal conductivity within 10–17 W/(K·m).
